deep.reconstruction:
Folio 6v has no legible mathematical content. The image shows about 30–35 extremely faint rows of dotted, typescript-like marks. In density and layout they resemble the numerical star table on the adjacent folio, so they are most likely show-through or offset (ink transferred from a facing sheet). No characters, numbers or formulas can be read with confidence, so I cannot reconstruct any derivation from this page.

The context pages show what the surrounding material is. It is an astronomical reduction table for a transit (meridian) instrument with seven threads. Each row gives a star, its declination δ and log cos δ, written in the 10-shifted form 10 + log10 cos δ. For example, for α Aquarii, δ = −1°1'56.79" gives 9.9999295. The row then gives six values of log(T_i / cos δ) = log T_i − log cos δ.

The T_i are the equatorial thread intervals in seconds, listed in the row headed 0°: 41.40952, 28.30722, 13.92315, 14.30539, 29.06280 and 41.65485. Their logarithms are 1.6171002, 1.4518972, 1.1437375, 1.1554997, 1.4633374 and 1.6196655. (My reading: these are the intervals between consecutive threads, or from each side thread to the middle thread. The two halves are unequal, about 83.64 s and 85.02 s, which suggests the middle thread is slightly off-centre.)

The page computes the standard reduction of thread intervals to a star of declination δ: t_i(δ) = T_i · sec δ. The previous page covers δ up to about 28°, and the next page continues from α Cygni (+44°45') to β UMi (+74°45'). Folio 6v presumably carried nothing, or only the illegible faint traces. My suggestion: it may once have held the intermediate declinations, about 28°–44°, but this cannot be confirmed from the image.
errors: None can be assessed on this page; nothing is legible.
In the adjacent pages, spot checks of log cos δ agree with modern values to about 1–2 units in the 7th decimal (e.g. α CMi: computed 9.9979243 vs. written 9.9979245).

results.usually_credited_to: Standard practical astronomy (18th–19th c.; e.g. Bessel, Gauss's Göttingen observatory practice)
